item.title: [8] Atomic functional site scaffolding in biopolymers with RFdiffusion3
item.description:
Score 8/10 · Science

RFdiffusion3 uses free-atom diffusion to satisfy atomic-level constraints for enzyme and RNA design with experimental validation, an RFdiffusion-lineage conditional generation advance whose constraint-satisfaction ideas could transfer to your steering work.

Jasper Butcher, Rohith Krishna, Raktim Mitra, Seth M. Woodbury, Donghyo Kim, Rafael I. Brent, Yanjing Li, Nathaniel Corley, Andrew Favor, Anqi Chen, Paul T. Kim, Jonathan Funk, Gabriela Bastidas Reinoso, Kejia Wu, Aiko Muraishi, Helen E. Eisenach, Saman Salike, Simon Mathis, Tuscan Rock Thompson, Antonia Ruder, Enisha Sehgal, Andrew Kubaney, Jie Chen, Yuliya Politanska, Brian Coventry, Odin Zhang, Florence J. Hardy, Bo Qiang, Kieran Didi, Maxwell Kazman, Lars L. Schaaf, Frank DiMaio, David Baker

The catalytic and other sophisticated functions of biomolecules arise from the placement of many atoms in three-dimensional space. Here, we describe a generative artificial intelligence method for biopolymers, RFdiffusion3 (RFD3), which employs free atom diffusion to satisfy complex sets of atomic constraints more rapidly and accurately than previous methods across several challenges from enzyme design to RNA structure design. We demonstrate experimentally the power of the RFD3 pipeline for enzyme design by designing de novo phosphotriesterases with a complex active site architecture incorporating a carbamylated lysine coordinating two metal ions and zinc proteases specific for the transthyretin protein involved in amyloid diseases; in both cases we obtain active catalysts in zero shot 96 construct design campaigns.

item.title: [9] When the Prior Is Wrong: Probing Misspecified Diffusion Priors in Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Probing misspecified diffusion priors in scientific inverse problems (seismic and black-hole imaging) via an amortized posterior over plausible discrepancies directly addresses the question of when a generative prior conflicts with experimental data, which is central to steering structure models.

Frederic Wang, Katherine L. Bouman

arXiv:2604.21066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While diffusion priors generate high-quality posterior samples across many scientific inverse problems, they are often trained on purely simulated data, thus inheriting the errors and biases of these underlying sources. Many approaches to adapting diffusion priors from a single observation require sufficient conflict between the data and the prior to successfully adapt and do not allow specific misspecification hypotheses to be tested. On the other hand, existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods determine whether the observation is compatible with a fixed prior, rather than specifying which assumptions to relax or by how much. To address these issues, we propose PIVOT: Prior Inference Via Observation-driven Transformations, which formulates diffusion prior misspecification as inference over an underlying latent variable representing a scientifically plausible discrepancy. By expanding the prior along these plausible directions of misspecification, PIVOT infers a posterior over the strength of each proposed discrepancy given the observation. This process can be efficiently amortized with just one posterior sampling pass using a conditional diffusion model. We also demonstrate how to determine if a proposed discrepancy is inconclusive because the measurement is too noisy or ill-posed. We validate PIVOT on seismic imaging and real-world black hole imaging problems, where we find that OOD observations generally lead to larger perturbation strengths when the proposed discrepancy family captures relevant components of the mismatch, as long as the discrepancy is visible to the measurement. PIVOT thereby provides an interpretable probe into how real-world priors could be misspecified.

item.title: [9] Guidance as Variance Matching
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Variance-matched guidance gives a closed-form rule that reproduces hand-picked guidance scales and offers a new mechanistic account of why guidance works, which you should see for any guided sampling in your steering platform.

Ali Backour, Artem Lukoianov, Frank Permenter, Tommi Jaakkola, Justin Solomon, Vincent Sitzmann

arXiv:2611.34801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Guidance repels the prediction of a diffusion model away from a weaker reference prediction. It substantially improves sample quality, but its mechanism remains poorly understood. We first find that, at the scales used in practice, guidance does not improve the prediction of the posterior mean (the model's training target); it makes the prediction worse, while samples improve. Second, posterior-mean predictions have less variance than the data, and we find that guidance restores it. We introduce variance-matched guidance: a closed-form rule that picks the guidance scale by matching the variance of the guided predictions to that of the data. Without tuning, it recovers the hand-picked scales of eleven widely used models across image, video, audio, motion, and world generation; to our knowledge, no previous explanation of guidance predicts them. Applied per noise level, it yields a schedule without tuned hyperparameters that users prefer to hand-crafted ones on SD 3.5 Medium. Third, we offer an interpretation of the mechanism behind guidance: each model makes a random error in predicting the posterior mean, and guidance rescales the difference of these errors into a sample with the posterior's covariance, which improves sampling. This view also suggests two new hypotheses that our experiments support: guidance can work with negative scales, and guiding a model with its own checkpoint needs a larger scale than guiding it with an independently trained model.

item.title: [9] AlloGen: Conformation-Selective Binder Generation with Differential State Scoring
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

AlloGen guides frozen backbone generators with a differential state score to get conformation-selective binders, validated by BLI on calmodulin, and combines state-conditioned guidance without retraining with ensemble awareness, which you would want to see.

Hanqun Cao, Aastha Pal, Sumi Kimura, Yesol Kim, Jingjie Zhang, Pheng Ann Heng, Pranam Chatterjee

arXiv:2606.05474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Protein binder design commonly optimizes compatibility with a single receptor conformation, leaving preference over alternative functional states unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce AlloGen, a modular method that decouples backbone generation from state-selectivity scoring. We train its SE(3)-invariant interface graph transformer, $Q_\theta$, through interface-quality regression followed by paired conformational discrimination. By comparing scores across states, we rerank candidates and guide frozen backbone generators without retraining. On a benchmark of 65 targets spanning 15 protein families, $Q_\theta$ achieved a mean Spearman correlation of $0.520$ on eight held-out targets. All 15 evaluated generator-guidance combinations achieved positive predicted selectivity averaged over these targets, and RFdiffusion with Langevin refinement reached $\bar{S}_{\mathrm{cons}}=0.677$ on calmodulin (CaM). To test the predicted preference experimentally, we measured binding by bio-layer interferometry. Five designed peptides bound holo CaM, with the strongest measured $K_D$ of 46.6 nM, and none showed detectable apo CaM binding under the tested conditions. Together, these results support computational prioritization of conformation-selective binders.

item.title: [8] Zero-Shot Generation of Protein Conformational Ensembles Through AlphaFold Latent Flooding
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

AlphaFold latent flooding generates conformational ensembles zero-shot at test time by exploring AF's latent space, directly in your territory of using structure predictors to sample multiple states.

QIAN, R., Zhan, R., Song, Z., Huang, J.

Despite transformative advances in protein structure prediction, generating conformational ensembles directly from sequence in an efficient and accessible manner remains a central challenge. We introduce a heuristic importance sampling framework for the zero-shot prediction of functionally relevant, conformationally diverse structures, bypassing the need for extensive physics-based modeling or prior domain knowledge. Guided by an analysis of massive activations in AlphaFold (AF), we develop a latent flooding algorithm that enables adversarial exploration of the latent space while preserving local geometric integrity. We show that the AF latent flooding (AFLF) method robustly recovers experimental structural fluctuations, captures function-relevant conformational states, and reveals cryptic binding sites across diverse protein systems. These results suggest that the AF latent space encodes functionally relevant conformational variability in a structured form that is readily amenable to post hoc exploration. Finally, we show that AFLF is computationally accessible and interoperable, offering a test-time generalization of AF for investigating protein dynamics and accelerating structure-based ligand discovery.

item.title: [7] Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Selective anchoring wraps pretrained diffusion and flow samplers so measured components are protected from the prior, with coverage guarantees, a direct analogue of how data-consistency should constrain a generative prior in your steering platform, though the application is medical imaging.

Nicolas Tricard, Stefan Brandst\"atter, Jason Chen, Zituo Chen, Linzheng Wang, Georg Langs, Sili Deng

arXiv:2611.33331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

item.title: [7] Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Closed-form analysis of classifier-free guidance on Gaussian mixtures explains mode collapse and concentration, which is useful theory for the guidance behavior in your steering work, though it is not about experimental-data conditioning.

Daniel Pfrommer, Chenyang Yuan, Frank Permenter, Ali Jadbabaie

arXiv:2611.33719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.

item.title: [10] Integrating hydrogen-exchange experiments with conformational ensembles
item.description:
Score 10/10 · bioRxiv

Lindorff-Larsen lab develops an HX forward model and uses HX as a restraint for reweighting ensembles from MD and generative AI models, squarely on your ensemble-plus-experimental-data theme.

Streit, J. O., Peterle, D., Tesei, G., Invernizzi, M. et al.

Protein conformational dynamics are central to biological function but remain difficult to characterise at scale. Amide hydrogen exchange (HX), measured by NMR or mass spectrometry, probes these dynamics but requires computational models for integration with structural ensembles. We benchmark models for calculating HX from ensembles using a large literature-derived dataset spanning folded and intrinsically disordered proteins. We then develop a model that identifies exchange-competent amides from local structural descriptors while accounting for electrostatic effects. The model predicts protection across a broad dynamic range in ensembles generated by molecular dynamics and generative AI. HX-guided ensemble reweighting improves agreement with independent NMR, SAXS, and folding-stability measurements. Millisecond HX distinguishes and refines alternative ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, while reweighting of structured proteins reveals folding intermediates and low-population excited states. These results establish HX as a quantitative restraint for ensemble reweighting and provide a scalable framework for benchmarking simulations and generative protein models.

item.title: [9] APEs: Agentic Prediction of Epitopes to Guide Antibody-Antigen Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Uses agent-derived epitope predictions to steer Protenix-v1 sampling for antibody-antigen complexes, an inference-time steering of a cofolding model with an external signal that is very close to sampleworks.

Kang, M., Yoon, M. S., Park, J., Moon, B. et al.

Antibody-antigen complex prediction remains difficult because the surface recognized by a specific antibody is often uncertain, and model confidence may not distinguish alternative poses. We developed APEs (Agentic Prediction of Epitopes for Structure Prediction), an agentic system that retrieves public evidence, interprets predicted antibody and antigen structures, and produces ranked residue-level epitope hypotheses. For retrospective evaluation, web retrieval was restricted to sources released before each CASP target entry date. Across eight CASP16 and six released CASP17 targets, the top-ranked patch reached residue precision of at least 0.5 for nine of 14 targets. We then used the predicted epitopes to steer additional Protenix-v1 sampling and to compare steered finalists with the highest ipSAE unsteered model. The retrospective best selection across three independent router calls increased mean DockQ from 0.306 to 0.375; DockQ increased from 0.089 to 0.679 for H2321 and from 0.005 to 0.379 for H2346. These results show that publicly available evidence specific to the target antibody-antigen complex can serve as an inference-time signal for epitope localization, guided complex sampling, and model selection. We also release predictions for CASP17 targets whose experimental structures had not been released when the predictions were finalized, providing a prospective test of APEs (https://github.com/CSSB-SNU/ape).

item.title: [9] XSSDense: X-ray Solution Scattering Density Reconstruction Using a Variational Autoencoder
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Reconstructs electron densities from SAXS/time-resolved scattering using a VAE prior trained on predicted ensembles, directly bridging generative priors and experimental data for conformational heterogeneity, as in your steering work.

Monrroy, L., Cardoch, S., Lee, S., Westenhoff, S.

Solution X-ray scattering reveals the structure of biomolecules in solution. Scattering profiles also encode information on conformational heterogeneity and, when measured with time resolution, transient structural intermediates. However, this information is difficult to access because scattering profiles contain limited information, and their interpretation largely relies on fitting candidate structures guided by prior knowledge. Direct reconstruction of electron densities has remained challenging because of the difficulty of incorporating such priors. Here we introduce XSSDense, which combines a variational autoencoder trained on electron densities from predicted or modelled protein ensembles with genetic optimization to refine densities against scattering data. We verify the method on synthetic data and apply it to time-resolved scattering experiments, recovering the conformational heterogeneity of the unfolded state of \emph{As}LOV2, resolving a de novo density of its pre-unfolding intermediate, and characterizing the signalling-state ensemble of photoactive yellow protein. We further demonstrate its application to conventional SAXS by refining different conformations of adenylate kinase. XSSDense enables structurally grounded electron density reconstructions that intrinsically capture conformational heterogeneity

item.title: [8] PRETZEL: A Benchmark for Cyclic Peptide Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

PRETZEL benchmarks AlphaFold3, Boltz-2 and Protenix-v2 on 285 cyclic peptide complexes and shows that low RMSD hides chemically invalid structures, which is exactly the kind of cofolding failure analysis and validation methodology you track.

Yongchan Hong, Zihang Fang, Mukta Ubale, Yan Liu, Xingyao Chen, Vsevolod Katritch

arXiv:2611.31708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, and co-folding models are increasingly used to predict their structures. Yet published evaluations rely on small, loosely curated target sets that differ from paper to paper, so results are not comparable, and most report pose RMSD alone, without checking whether the predicted molecule is chemically correct. We introduce PRETZEL (Prediction of Ring-Enclosed Topology: Zero-shot Evaluation of cycLic peptides), a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes spanning three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoff of every model evaluated. PRETZEL has three components: PRETZEL-SET, an evaluation set annotated by cyclization chemistry and chemical novelty; PRETZEL-TWIST, a specification layer that compiles a single canonical macrocycle description into each engine's native input format and verifies the returned structure; and PRETZEL-SALT, an evaluation suite pairing standard pose metrics with validity checks for bond distances, bond angles, dihedrals, and ring closure. Using these, we evaluate AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Protenix-v2, and HighFold3. Protenix-v2 achieves the best median RMSD at 9.05 A, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 A and 37.5% under 5 A. Accuracy varies by cyclization chemistry: models handle head-to-tail macrocycles relatively well but degrade on stapled targets. Chemical validity is weaker still: at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions, so pose accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion. These failures share a cause: co-folding models place macrocycles without representing them, treating cyclization and non-canonical chemistry as annotations layered onto a residue sequence rather than as first-class structure. PRETZEL is released with all inputs, predictions, and evaluation code.

item.title: [8] The physical foundation beneath protein generative modeling
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A review arguing that protein generative models need physics and should be updated with experimental data speaks directly to the premise of data-steered generative structure models.

Tianyu Lu, Po-Ssu Huang

arXiv:2609.04465v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Physical equations in protein modeling appear to have been replaced by generative models trained directly on structure data. By learning a mapping from noise to data, sampling de novo protein structures has become much more efficient. However, such models can also learn non-physical features and break down with out-of-distribution settings which are typical in protein design campaigns. In this review, we highlight where the physics persists in protein generative modeling pipelines and the issues that linger when physically relevant components of a macromolecular system are left unmodeled. We present a perspective that respecting the underlying physics of macromolecular systems, increasingly through learned representations that are physically grounded and updating generative models with experimental data, is foundational to generative modeling for functional protein design.

item.title: [7] Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
item.description:
Score 7/10 · Nature

Nature reports that general-purpose Claude and ChatGPT models can now design proteins and predict sequences and structures, which bears directly on how you think about specialized cofolding models versus general agents.

Ewen Callaway

Anthropic and OpenAI’s language models can design proteins and predict their sequences and structures — capabilities previously seen only in specialized AI tools.

item.title: [7] Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

PathGrad's stable gradients through Langevin path probabilities for refining ML force fields against experimental observables directly address integrating experimental data into physical models, which parallels your experiment-guided ensemble work.

Zhongyao Wang, Lun Song, Yakun Zeng, Xingao Gong, Rui Shi, Mao Su

arXiv:2611.32851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.

item.title: [7] EM-Claw: An Experience-Grounded Language-Model Agent for Auto Cryo-EM Single-Particle Analysis
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

A multi-agent system that autonomously runs CryoSPARC/RELION pipelines and handles heterogeneity and flexibility is a serious science-agent for structural biology you would want to see.

Shan, H., Li, J., Xing, Z., Yuan, Q. et al.

Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) processing remains strongly dependent on expert judgement because difficult specimens often require dataset-specific strategies that cannot be captured by a fixed pipeline. Here we present EM-Claw, an experience-grounded multi-agent system for adaptive cryo-EM single-particle analysis. Rather than following a predefined workflow, EM-Claw retrieves processing precedents from previously solved datasets, consults external guidance, proposes and independently evaluates alternative strategies, executes CryoSPARC or RELION jobs, and revises the processing route according to quantitative and visual evidence. Human expertise can be introduced at any stage through natural-language instructions, while successful decisions and processing trajectories are retained as reusable experience. We evaluated EM-Claw on both publicly available cryo-EM datasets and experimental datasets collected in our laboratory, spanning soluble proteins, membrane proteins, GPCR complexes and small transporter monomers. Across these cases, EM-Claw adapted its processing strategies to specimen-specific challenges, including compositional heterogeneity, complex flexibility, preferred orientation and weak particle features. It produced reconstructions at higher resolution than previously published results (0.1~1.3 angstroms improvement) or solved structures that are now being prepared for publication, with no or little human intervention, thereby substantially reducing the time, effort and field experience required for human decision-making.

item.title: [10] What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
item.description:
Score 10/10 · arXiv

Transition path sampling over Boltz-2 denoising trajectories to probe ensembles and memorization versus learned physics is squarely in your cofolding-ensemble and critique interests and you would be surprised to have missed it.

Muhammad R. Hasyim

arXiv:2611.30062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

item.title: [8] Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Gradient-free Stein Guidance with whole-path Metropolis-Hastings correction proposes a genuinely new inference-time reward-steering scheme that overcomes SMC particle scaling, directly relevant to steering diffusion models with non-differentiable rewards.

Youheng Zhu, Chenyang Wang, Minshuo Chen, Yiping Lu

arXiv:2611.28654v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

item.title: [8] Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A theoretical account of how classifier-free guidance amplifies score errors via a Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition bears directly on understanding guidance in diffusion models like those you steer.

Pengyu Luo, Yisha Yao, Bolun Li

arXiv:2611.28451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

item.title: [8] Estimating Extrapolation Factors in Time-Resolved Crystallography
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A principled, physically constrained estimator of triggered-state density in time-resolved crystallography with a reusable package is highly relevant to experimental density handling and heterogeneity, and likely useful for density-guided ensemble work.

Sebastian Bielfeldt, Henry N. Chapman, Thomas J. Lane

arXiv:2611.28961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved crystallography (TRX) captures macromolecules in action, but a triggered crystal contains a mixture of triggered proteins in an unknown state and untriggered proteins in the reference state. Separating these is necessary to isolate the dynamics of interest and is an underdetermined data-analysis task. For the simplest case, with one triggered state and one reference state, a range of methods exists, but their assumptions, accuracy, and domains of applicability have not been systematically investigated. Here, we deconstruct and review the methods in current use, employing a unified notation. We make their assumptions explicit and benchmark each on a simulated dataset. A key point is that many of these methods do not estimate the fraction of all triggered molecules in the crystal, but instead estimate a latent parameter we call the extrapolation factor, which is related to but distinct from the so-called "occupancy". As our simulations make apparent, current methods do not always yield accurate results, in particular with noisy data and when the fraction of triggered protein is low. Inspired by previous work, we introduce Vacuum Level Matching, a method that grounds the estimate in the physical constraint that electron density is a nonnegative quantity: it cannot fall below a vacuum level. Operating voxel by voxel, Vacuum Level Matching replaces the manual choices of previous methods with a data-driven procedure and reports quality-control metrics that flag data unable to support a confident prediction. On the same simulated data, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and on two experimental datasets, rsEGFP2 and a multi-time-point photolyase series, it recovers known structural changes while flagging issues where the data are weak. Finally, we report an implementation of Vacuum Level Matching in the form of a small, reusable Python package.

item.title: [8] Towards Accurate Prediction of Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein Structure
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Benchmarking AlphaFold3 against wild-type/mutant crystal pairs shows accuracy dropping with deformation magnitude, a directly relevant failure analysis for cofolding models on subtle conformational changes.

Zhuoyi Liu, Alex Calabrese, Corey S. O'Hern

arXiv:2609.24842v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proteins can possess numerous mutations relative to their wild-type amino acid sequences with minimal impact to their structure and function. However, in other cases, even a single amino acid mutation relative to the wild-type sequence can lead to a large change in structure or even a disease phenotype. While the accuracy of wild-type protein structure prediction has improved significantly in recent years, it remains difficult to accurately predict the structure of mutant proteins. Here, we characterize the local mutation-induced structural changes in proteins for a dataset of wildtype and the corresponding single-amino acid mutant x-ray crystal structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We find that mutation-induced structural changes in these proteins are localized at the site of the mutation, decaying rapidly with increasing spatial distance from the mutation site. In addition, we evaluate how well AlphaFold3 can recapitulate the observed mutation-induced structural deformations in the x-ray crystal structures. We find that the accuracy of the AlphaFold3 predictions decreases strongly with increasing mutation-induced deformation. In contrast to the results for AlphaFold3, the Pearson correlation between a single physical feature, i.e. the change in solvent accessibility, and the mutation-induced deformation does not depend on the magnitude of the deformation. Our results and analyses provide a framework for further studies aimed at predicting the structural changes in proteins caused by single amino acid mutations.

item.title: [7] A Tutorial on Diffusion Theory: From Differential Equations to Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A self-contained tutorial deriving diffusion models from SDEs, reverse-time dynamics and classifier and classifier-free guidance matches the long-form mathematical exposition you wanted flagged.

Jiayi Fu, Yuxia Wang

arXiv:2605.22586v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a leading framework for generative modeling, yet their mathematical foundations are often presented in separate treatments. This tutorial offers a unified, self-contained introduction organized into three parts. First, we construct a forward generative stochastic differential equation (SDE) that transports noise to data, marginalize over the clean data endpoint, and derive training objectives directly from the forward dynamics. Second, we begin with a conditional path from data to noise, marginalize it to obtain the forward process, and derive the corresponding reverse-time SDE and training objectives. Within this forward-reverse framework, we also establish the connection between denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) and variance-preserving (VP) SDEs. Third, we review numerical methods for solving SDEs and discuss two approaches to guided generation: classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance.

item.title: [7] Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A Feynman-Kac weight reduction for stable sampling of products of diffusion experts is a new guidance idea with molecular sampling experiments, relevant to composing multiple restraints.

Sunjin Kim, Sungsoo Ahn, Michael Chertkov

arXiv:2611.29764v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $\beta_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $\lambda$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\beta_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $\lambda=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $\lambda\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $\lambda=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $\lambda=1/B$ perform better empirically.

item.title: [10] BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
item.description:
Score 10/10 · arXiv

BioEmu2 extends the equilibrium-ensemble emulator to multi-component complexes with time propagation and explicit conditioning/bias-potential steering, so you would be surprised not to have seen it.

Michael Gastegger, Adam E. Foster, Jos\'e Jim\'enez-Luna, Tim Hempel, Sarah Lewis, Yu Xie, Lixin Sun, Iryna Zaporozhets, J. Thorben Frank, Yaoyi Chen, Michael Plainer, Ludwig Winkler, Pedro B. P. S. Reis, Sven H. Giese, Roberto Sordillo, Victor Garc\'ia Satorras, Eray Inanc, Kacper Kapu\'sniak, Soojung Yang, Rishwanth Raghu, Rachel Kim, Gabriel Dernbach, Deniz Gunceler, Hannes Schulz, Bonnie Kruft, Marwin Segler, Christopher M. Bishop, Cecilia Clementi, Ryota Tomioka, Frank No\'e

arXiv:2611.27924v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

item.title: [9] Structural Agreement Indicates Prediction Accuracy For Protein-Ligand Co-Folding
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Shows that confidence scores across seven cofolding models barely beat random selection and that structural agreement among sampled predictions (CORE) is a far better reliability signal, directly relevant to evaluating cofolding and ensemble sampling.

J. Henry Broster, Bojana Popovic, Diana Kondinskaia, Charlotte M. Deane, Fergus Imrie

arXiv:2611.27058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Co-folding models predict the structures of proteins and their bound ligands, but their accuracy varies across targets. Their usefulness therefore depends on knowing which predictions a user can trust. Confidence scores are intended to guide that choice. However, across seven co-folding models, we show that confidence-based selection offers little improvement over choosing a prediction at random. For approximately three-quarters of structures, predictions are either exclusively correct or incorrect, leaving no opportunity for ranking to change the outcome. Moreover, high confidence does not reliably discriminate correct top-ranked predictions from incorrect ones. We find that structural agreement among predictions is a more accurate measure of likely success than current confidence scores. We capture this with the Concentration of Repeated Ensembles (CORE) Score, which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support. CORE Score discriminates top-1 success and oracle success, achieving mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, compared to 0.757 and 0.759 for ipTM. CORE Score also outperforms training set similarity measures, including ligand Tanimoto, protein sequence, and Runs N' Poses similarity, despite requiring no experimental ligand pose. Structural agreement is therefore a practical indicator of reliability and a baseline for evaluating future confidence estimators, without requiring an additional trained uncertainty estimator.

item.title: [7] Inpainting physics: self-supervised learning for context-driven fluid simulation
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Learning a self-supervised flow-matching prior and imposing constraints only at inference by fixing known regions is the same inverse-problem-with-generative-prior pattern you use, albeit demonstrated on CFD rather than structures.

Jonas Weidner, Yeray Martin-Ruisanchez, Daniel Rueckert, Benedikt Wiestler, Julian Suk

arXiv:2605.08832v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are typically trained as forward operators that map explicit problem specifications, such as geometry and boundary conditions, to solution fields. This ties the model to the conditioning variables seen during training and limits reuse under boundary-condition shifts or local geometry changes. We propose to reformulate steady CFD inference as an inpainting problem: instead of training on explicit boundary conditions, we learn a self-supervised prior over velocity fields and impose boundary constraints only during inference by fixing known regions such as inlet, outlet or unchanged regions from previous simulations. To scale this idea to large 3D meshes, we introduce a local neighbourhood tokeniser that represents high-resolution velocity fields as compact spatial latent tokens and train latent flow-matching and masked-autoencoder models on these tokens. On simulations of intracranial aneurysm flow, our method reconstructs full velocity fields from sparse boundary context, outperforms supervised neural surrogates under boundary-condition and dataset shift and enables local geometry editing by reusing unchanged simulation context. These results suggest that viewing CFD inference as context-conditioned inpainting can turn neural surrogates from task-specific predictors into reusable flow priors. Code and demo are available at https://inpainting-physics.com.

item.title: [7] Learning to Assimilate: Amortized Control for Autoregressive Diffusion
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Training a lightweight stochastic-optimal-control controller on a frozen diffusion prior to steer samples toward sparse observations without per-sample optimization is directly analogous to amortized data-guided steering of structure models.

Prakhar Srivastava, Farrin Marouf Sofian, Francesco Immorlano, Kushagra Pandey, Stephan Mandt

arXiv:2510.06637v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autoregressive diffusion models (ARDMs) offer expressive priors for forecasting chaotic dynamics. However, maintaining consistency with sparse observations over long rollouts can require substantial test-time computation. We introduce Control-Augmented Data Assimilation (CADA), which trains a lightweight controller on top of a frozen ARDM to steer predictions toward future observations. Using a KL-regularized stochastic optimal control objective, the controller learns from short autoregressive rollouts to anticipate observations while staying close to the pretrained dynamics. At inference, it injects corrections at each denoising step without per-forecast optimization. Across two chaotic PDE benchmarks, CADA improves long-horizon accuracy, stability, and physical fidelity under sparse observations. On compact ERA5, it outperforms diffusion-based baselines in most regimes with over $10\times$ faster inference than conditional diffusion baselines. Applied to frozen GenCast, CADA also reduces temperature errors across 12--48-hour forecasts with spatially sparse observations. Code is available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/cada.

item.title: [7] AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Diffusion-based posterior sampling that corrects likelihood guidance via the conditional Tweedie identity with ensemble proposals is a genuinely new take on inverse problems with diffusion priors, directly transferable to data-conditioned steering.

Yangwen Zhang, Shiwei Ni, Xiaoping Zhang, Xiaofei Guan, Lili Ju

arXiv:2609.32411v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.

item.title: [7] Predicted templates improve the prediction of antibody-antigen structures by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Template-augmented AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2 for antibody-antigen docking is a useful cofolding failure-mode study with a cheap way to expand sampling, though it is a narrow application rather than a general method.

Ziaee, O., Lazou, M., Joseph-McCarthy, D., Vajda, S.

Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

item.title: [7] Sequence-Derived Geometric Priors Enable Controllable Generation of Intrinsically Disordered Protein Ensembles
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

MANTA generates controllable IDP conformational ensembles from sequence-derived geometric priors and shows that prior estimation is the bottleneck, which is directly relevant to ensemble generation and conditioning, though it is a sequence-to-ensemble model with a graph-Laplacian decoder rather than a cofolding or experimental-data-steered approach.

Jang, W., Shin, W.-H.

Predicting heterogeneous conformational ensembles from sequence remains a central challenge for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Sequence-to-ensemble models often entangle geometric inference with coordinate generation, obscuring error sources and limiting control over ensemble properties. Here we introduce MANTA, a C-level framework that separates these stages. An encoder derives geometric priors from protein language-model representations, and a graph-Laplacian decoder converts these priors into conformational ensembles. On a homology-held-out test set, replacing predicted priors with reference-derived priors under the same decoder reduces the median absolute relative radius-of-gyration error from 8.78% to 1.89%, identifying geometric-prior estimation as the dominant bottleneck in MANTA. Across an external benchmark of 27 IDPs, MANTA generates broad, locally valid ensembles. Decoder controls modulate mean compactness and conformational breadth along partially separable axes, while compactness modulation alters motif exposure in tau and amyloid-{beta}. Meanwhile, -synuclein variants shift local exposure populations at nearly unchanged global size. MANTA provides a diagnostic and controllable framework for ensemble generation that captures both global dimensions and local conformational organization.
